newsitem.title: USA: President proposes plan to revitalize DC business.
newsitem.headline: President proposes plan to revitalize DC business.

text.p: President Clinton Tuesday called for $300 million in federal financial aid to encourage companies in the nation's capital to turn vacant lots and crumbling buildings into viable businesses.
"(This) city is every American's home and should be every American's pride," Clinton said at a White House press briefing.
"We must help our capital city lift itself to a point where it can be a model for revitalisation. Now is the time."

Clinton proposed creating a new Economic Development Corporation that would provide millions of dollars in tax breaks to private businesses to set up in distressed District of Columbia neighbourhoods and to hire low-income residents.
"Washington started as a planned city," Clinton said. " Washington, Jefferson and (Pierre) L'Enfant shared a vision of order and beauty."
"But this is a different time and the city needs a new vision -- one that touches our schools, streets and one that makes busineses want to locate (and) create jobs here."
Clinton said the new corporation would get $50 million to start up and $250 million in tax breaks and other incentives that it could use to help companies to locate in the city.
For instance, the corporation would let companies that invested in or made loans to D.C. businesses deduct 25 percent of those costs from federal taxes.
It also would give District businesses a 40 percent tax break on the first $10,000 they paid each low or moderate income resident in the first year of employment.
Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a troubled city of 543,000 people, many poor and black.
After years of budget shortfalls and mismanagement, Congress in 1995 turned over the finances of the cash-starved capital to a special control board.

But the city's problems are stubborn. Services remain erratic or non-existent, a former U.S. army general had to be appointed to run its schools, fire trucks and emergency vehicles are in short supply, police cars go unrepaired, potholes unfilled and crime flourishes.
"For too long, the federal government has kept its distance" from the District, Vice President Al Gore said at the press briefing.
"It's a shame. This is the capital of our nation. It is the face we present to the entire world. It is a place we should showcase," Gore said.
